newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Forty dead, 20,000 affected by Afghan floods.
newsitem.headline: Forty dead, 20,000 affected by Afghan floods.

text.p: Up to 40 people have been killed and 20,000 affected by floods in 10 provinces in northern Afghanistan, according to United Nations and Red Cross reports.

"At least 10 provinces in northern Afghanistan, covering 20 percent of the country, are affected by flooding," reported a bulletin released by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Kabul on Thursday.
The Federation report added another 16 dead to a United Nations total of 24 released on Wednesday.
"More than 20,000 victims have been reported affected; many having lost their homes and most of their belongings," said the Federation bulletin.
It said that the flooding started on April 22, but that the full extent of the damage is still unclear.

"Survey teams are still in the field and the full extent of the flood is not yet known. Several of the most affected areas are remote and difficult to reach by road, partly because of the floods. Preliminary reports have been received from nine provinces," it says.
The Federation report says the floods have caused widespread damage to infrastructure and agriculture.
"The floods have caused extensive damage to agricultural land, destroyed crops nnd washed away livestock and homes," the Federation said.
The Federation and U.N. reports show a total of over 1,500 houses damaged, 2,500 livestock killed and 7,100 hectares (17,750 acres) of farmland under water.
The Federation bulletin says it has started aid distributions in collaboration with the International Committee of the Red Cross in Faryab province.
"So far 1,000 blankets, 300 bales of used clothes, 10 tonnes of flour, and 40 family rations have been distributed," the bulletin reported.
"The most immediate priorities are food and shelter. Second priority will be tents, tarpaulins, plastic sheeting and clothing as well as some medecines," it said.
The United Nations also expects to start food distributions in the near future, a spokeswoman said.
"The U.N. World Food Programme says it has 500 tonnes of wheat standing by for this kind of event and will provide food immediately to Sholgara (village in Balkh province)."
U.N. spokeswoman Sarah Russell said on Wednesday U.N. agencies and the U.K.-based aid agency Oxfam would repair bridges, mend canals and restore water supplies.
The Federation report blames the disaster on a combination of heavy rainfall and damage to the eco-system.

"Natural disasters such as this are the direct result of the lack of a long-term national policy in Afghanistan to maintain the mountain eco-system. Deforestation, poor water catchment, over-grazing and ploughing of mountain slopes are factors which continuously increase the risks for this kind of disaster," said the Federation bulletin.
